q01-c01.text: The scientific evidence points to the universe having a finite past.

q01-c02.text: Science does not say the universe had a beginning, and there is no evidence for one.

q01-c03.text: A survey of physicists found most of them do not think the Big Bang was an absolute beginning.

q01-c04.text: Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, so it has always existed and there was no beginning.

q01-c05.text: The expansion of the universe had a finite beginning, but something was already there to expand.

q01-c06.text: Because something cannot come from nothing, the universe must always have existed.

q01-c07.text: Having a finite past and having a beginning are two different claims.

q01-c08.text: Everything in the known universe oscillates, so the universe itself probably bounces rather than begins.

q01-c09.text: The Big Bang had a beginning, and matter existed before it.

q01-c10.text: Nothing inside the universe exceeds light speed, yet the universe's expansion does, so rules for things inside may not apply to the whole.

q01-c11.text: Anyone who relies on induction must conclude it is reasonable that the universe had a beginning.

q02-c01.text: Only things that begin to exist need a cause; a cause outside space and time looks a lot like what people mean by God.

q02-c02.text: Exempting God from needing a cause is special pleading; if beginnings need explaining, who made God?

q02-c03.text: The argument claims that nothing exists without a creator.

q02-c04.text: If God can exist uncaused, then in principle the universe can exist uncaused too.

q02-c05.text: Saying something caused the universe is a very different step from saying an immaterial, timeless, powerful mind caused it.

q02-c06.text: Everything that begins to exist has a natural cause.

q02-c07.text: Metaphysical conclusions cannot be proved with physics.

q02-c08.text: The first-cause argument amounts to filling a gap in knowledge with God.

q02-c09.text: None of the arguments points to the God of the Bible specifically.

q03-c01.text: The fundamental constants sit in an extremely narrow range that permits life at all.

q03-c02.text: The multiverse is unobserved, and many versions of it need fine-tuning of their own.

q03-c03.text: Almost all of the universe is instantly lethal to life, so it cannot be fine-tuned for life.

q03-c04.text: Any designer who tuned this mostly empty, hostile universe for life was incompetent.

q03-c05.text: Nobody has shown the constants could have taken other values, so calling the range narrow has no reference point.

q03-c06.text: We can only ever observe a universe compatible with our own existence, so observing one is unsurprising.

q03-c07.text: The odds of a universe like ours are 100 percent, because this is the universe we have.

q03-c08.text: Fine-tuning is the most compelling argument of the set, but at best it reaches deism, not Christianity.

q03-c09.text: Dismissing the multiverse as unobserved is inconsistent when God is also unobserved.

q03-c10.text: If the universe is tuned for anything, it is tuned for black holes rather than life.

q03-c11.text: Asking whether the universe is fine-tuned for life is like asking whether a puddle is fine-tuned for its pothole.

q04-c01.text: Torturing a child for fun is wrong everywhere and always, not merely unfashionable.

q04-c02.text: Objective moral facts need grounding in something beyond shifting human opinion.

q04-c03.text: The Euthyphro dilemma is a false choice because goodness is grounded in God's own nature.

q04-c04.text: The wrongness of child torture is a feeling, not a fact.

q04-c06.text: For any supposedly universal moral rule there is some society where breaking it is normal.

q04-c07.text: Some societies treat practices that harm children, such as circumcision or genital cutting, as morally acceptable.

q04-c08.text: There may be an objectively correct moral answer that we simply do not know.

q04-c09.text: Statements about minds cannot be true independently of minds, so morality cannot be mind-independent.

q04-c10.text: There is no independent way to establish that God's nature is good rather than simply defining it as good.

q04-c11.text: Grounding goodness in God's nature does not escape the Euthyphro problem.

q04-c12.text: Every social species has morality to some degree, so morality is a product of social evolution.

q04-c13.text: Skeptics dodge the direct question of whether killing a baby is morally wrong.

q05-c01.text: The Old Testament has God command the Israelites to kill their enemies' children on several occasions.

q05-c02.text: A video game can make it impossible to kill children; God could have done the same in the real world.

q05-c03.text: Drowning the world and an eternal hell are themselves torturous, which undercuts an objection to child torture.

q05-c04.text: Critics picture God as a movie character rather than engaging with classical theism.

q05-c05.text: Behaviours considered moral two centuries ago are not today, so morality shifts with culture.

q06-c02.text: There is little or no evidence that Jesus existed.

q06-c03.text: Only fringe people claim Jesus was a real person.

q06-c04.text: There is no historical proof of the crucifixion.

q06-c05.text: Historians are not convinced Jesus was crucified rather than impaled or hanged.

q06-c06.text: The Romans crucified hundreds of thousands of people, so Jesus would have been just one more.

q06-c07.text: Claiming hundreds witnessed the risen Jesus is like claiming hundreds witnessed a fictional character's death.

q06-c08.text: Jesus of Nazareth lived, preached and died; Jesus the miracle-working god did not.

q06-c09.text: That Jesus existed and was crucified is the view of virtually every expert on the subject.

q07-c01.text: The Gospels were written anonymously decades after the crucifixion and named a century later.

q07-c02.text: The earliest Gospel, Mark, originally had no post-resurrection appearances.

q07-c03.text: All of the Gospels were anonymous and written under false names.

q07-c04.text: The Gospels are fiction composed as rhetorical school exercises.

q07-c06.text: Even the professional historians of that era embellished or fabricated people and events.

q07-c07.text: The view that the Gospels are unreliable is not the historical consensus.

q08-c01.text: The creed preserved in 1 Corinthians 15 traces to within a few years of the events.

q08-c02.text: The creed is too early to be legend.

q08-c03.text: The claim that the creed dates to within a few years exists only in the imagination of apologists.

q08-c04.text: There are no creeds in the New Testament, including 1 Corinthians 15:3-8.

q08-c05.text: Reading the appearance to the five hundred as a mass vision over a crowd is a coherent and plausible interpretation.

q08-c06.text: Paul is the only first-hand witness, and what he describes seeing differs from the traditional resurrection narrative.

q08-c07.text: Paul never mentions an empty tomb, and the tomb's site is not mentioned until the fourth century.

q08-c08.text: An early source is not automatically a historically accurate one.

q08-c09.text: Skeptics' doubts about the creed are fear and accusation, not arguments.

q09-c01.text: Individuals hallucinate, but groups do not share the identical hallucination.

q09-c03.text: The appearances can be explained as independent people having separate grief hallucinations.

q09-c04.text: Tens of thousands of people agreed they saw the sun fall from the sky at Fatima, so groups can share a vision.

q09-c05.text: Many people share a false memory of a famous death, so shared mistaken beliefs are common.

q09-c06.text: A mother whose baby was taken by a dingo was telling the truth while millions disbelieved her, so majority disbelief proves nothing.

q09-c07.text: A Columbine martyr story spread and became accepted within a week, so legends can form almost instantly.

q09-c08.text: People believed Elvis was alive within days of his death.

q09-c09.text: An ancient figure, Peregrinus, had post-mortem appearance reports within a generation, so fast legends are documented.

q10-c01.text: The apostles were transformed and willing to die for something they claimed to have witnessed.

q10-c02.text: Even an apologist's own study finds only a handful of apostolic martyrdom stories hold up.

q10-c03.text: There is not enough data to be confident about the apostles' martyrdoms.

q10-c04.text: Historians grant how about three apostles died, and we do not know whether they could have recanted.

q10-c05.text: There are no reliable historical accounts of what happened to any apostle, including Peter and Paul.

q10-c06.text: Any claim that the apostles died for their beliefs is legend.

q10-c07.text: Up to four apostles may have been martyred, and some may have been punished for politics rather than belief.

q10-c08.text: Sincerity shows conviction, not that the belief was true.

q10-c09.text: Weak martyrdom evidence destroys the case for a bodily resurrection.

q11-c01.text: Committed skeptics such as Paul and James converted after claiming to encounter the risen Jesus.

q11-c02.text: Paul was not a skeptic about God; he held a different view of God.

q11-c03.text: As far as we can tell, Paul was a believer from the start.

q11-c04.text: There is no compelling evidence that James was a skeptic, and the 1 Corinthians 15 list seems to rule it out.

q11-c05.text: Someone like Paul would have seen himself as converted, not as adopting a new take on Judaism.

q12-c01.text: If the resurrection evidence counts, the same standard should accept the splitting of the moon or Joseph Smith's golden plates.

q12-c02.text: Thousands of early Muslims died for beliefs about Muhammad's miracles; consistency demands the same credit.

q12-c03.text: Apollonius of Tyana and Peregrinus also had reports of post-mortem appearances.

q12-c04.text: If the biblical stories came from a religion you did not already hold, you would not believe them.

q12-c05.text: Humans like to tell stories and can sincerely believe things that are not true.

q12-c06.text: The argument boils down to claiming everyone outside Christianity is lying.

q13-c01.text: Even if the resurrection happened, it would be evidence of an unusual healing ability, not of divinity.

q13-c02.text: A resurrection does not prove the divinity of the person raised; Elijah and Elisha performed such miracles too.

q13-c03.text: The being Paul saw might have been a demon rather than Jesus.

q14-c01.text: Each argument alone can be resisted, but stacked together the whole picture is hard to explain any other way.

q14-c02.text: Adding poor evidence together does not make good evidence.

q14-c03.text: An accumulation of zeros adds up to zero.

q14-c04.text: Stacking weak arguments does not make them more compelling.

q14-c05.text: Skeptics will dismiss inference to the best explanation as mere abduction.

q15-c01.text: Having a church community makes the believer feel more loved.

q15-c02.text: How being a Christian feels has no bearing on whether Christianity's claims are true.

q15-c03.text: The experience of community is the most compelling part of the case for Christianity.

q15-c04.text: Church communities have also taught people that being gay is evil, with devastating results.

q15-c05.text: A genuine skeptic would not repeat the same familiar apologetic arguments.

q15-c06.text: The real question is whether any of these arguments leads to intimacy with God.

q15-c07.text: Angry replies in the comments show the argument has hit a nerve.

q15-c08.text: Well-known apologists such as Ken Ham and Kent Hovind show what the Christian side relies on.
